title: Hyperinflation Shock
scenario: A sudden supply chain collapse causes food and energy prices to surge by 50%. Civil unrest is brewing in urban centers.

cards.title: Price Controls
cards.realWorldContext: Venezuela and Weimar Germany both capped prices during hyperinflation crises. It eases pain immediately, but producers often stop selling at a loss, causing shortages.
cards.policyExplanation: A government-mandated cap on how much sellers can charge for goods, meant to keep essentials affordable during a crisis.

cards.title: Raise Interest Rates
cards.realWorldContext: Modeled on the US Federal Reserve's rate hikes under Paul Volcker in the early 1980s, which broke double-digit inflation but triggered a sharp recession.
cards.policyExplanation: Making it more expensive to borrow money, which slows spending and cools inflation, but also slows the broader economy.

cards.title: Import Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: Governments like Egypt have long subsidized food imports to keep prices affordable. It works short-term but drains foreign currency reserves fast.
cards.policyExplanation: Government payments that lower the cost of imported goods, making them cheaper for consumers to buy.

cards.title: Rationing System
cards.realWorldContext: Britain and the US both rationed goods during World War II. It protects fair access but requires heavy enforcement and is deeply unpopular.
cards.policyExplanation: A formal limit on how much of a scarce good each person or household can buy, meant to ensure fair access.

cards.title: Export Restrictions
cards.realWorldContext: India and Russia have restricted grain exports during shortages to protect domestic supply, though this can breach trade agreements and invite retaliation.
cards.policyExplanation: Government limits or bans on selling certain goods abroad, keeping more of the domestic supply at home.

debrief: Pairing interest rate hikes to contain economic insolvency with targeted price controls provides the essential bridge to maintain political stability.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever combination stabilizes prices fastest for the most people, even if it means some producers lose out.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether the poorest, who suffer most from inflation, are protected first — favoring rationing or subsidies over policies that primarily help those with savings.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would object to price controls and rationing as coercive interference, arguing markets should be left to correct themselves.

title: Bank Liquidity Panic
scenario: Rumors of bad commercial loans spark a run on regional institutions, threatening bank defaults within 24 hours.

cards.title: Emergency Deposit Guarantee
cards.realWorldContext: Modeled on FDIC deposit insurance created after 1930s bank runs. It restores depositor confidence fast, but ultimately shifts risk onto taxpayers.
cards.policyExplanation: A government promise to reimburse depositors if their bank fails, meant to stop panicked withdrawals.

cards.title: Central Bank Liquidity Window
cards.realWorldContext: The Federal Reserve's discount window lends directly to solvent banks facing short-term cash shortages, stopping panic from becoming real insolvency.
cards.policyExplanation: A facility that lets banks borrow cash directly from the central bank when they're short on funds but not actually insolvent.

cards.title: Mandatory Bank Holidays
cards.realWorldContext: FDR closed every US bank for a 'bank holiday' in 1933 to halt withdrawals and audit banks before reopening. It stops the bleeding but freezes the economy.
cards.policyExplanation: A government order temporarily closing all banks to stop withdrawals while regulators assess which banks are actually solvent.

cards.title: Expropriate Bank Profits
cards.realWorldContext: Cyprus's 2013 'bail-in' forced depositors and bank shareholders to absorb losses directly. It raises funds without new borrowing, but punishes savers.
cards.policyExplanation: Forcing banks (or their shareholders and large depositors) to absorb losses directly, rather than using public funds to cover them.

cards.title: Interest Rate Cap
cards.realWorldContext: Capping interest rates limits how much banks can charge, echoing historical usury caps, but can also make it harder for banks to attract capital in a crisis.
cards.policyExplanation: A legal limit on how much interest banks can charge or pay, intended to control lending costs during a crisis.

debrief: Opening a Central Bank Liquidity Window solves institutional solvency while an Emergency Deposit Guarantee restores public confidence to halt retail bank runs.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whatever stops the panic fastest and protects the most depositors, even if it costs taxpayers.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would scrutinize who actually bears the cost — a bail-in that protects wealthy shareholders while ordinary depositors lose money would be unjust.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would argue failing banks should be allowed to fail, seeing bailouts as rewarding risky behavior at public expense.

title: Sovereign Debt Crunch
scenario: Foreign credit markets freeze following a default rumor. The national currency plummets, and foreign debt obligations are due in 48 hours.

cards.title: IMF Bailout Agreement
cards.realWorldContext: Greece (2010) and Argentina (repeatedly) received IMF emergency loans tied to reform conditions. It solves the immediate cash crunch but usually forces unpopular austerity.
cards.policyExplanation: An emergency loan from the International Monetary Fund, usually granted in exchange for economic reforms the borrowing country agrees to make.

cards.title: Emergency Capital Controls
cards.realWorldContext: Iceland (2008) and Greece (2015) restricted money leaving the country to stop capital flight, stabilizing the currency short-term at the cost of investor confidence.
cards.policyExplanation: Government restrictions on how much money can leave the country, meant to stop a rapid outflow of capital during a currency crisis.

cards.title: Sovereign Debt Restructuring
cards.realWorldContext: Argentina has restructured its sovereign debt multiple times, easing the immediate burden but often locking the country out of credit markets for years.
cards.policyExplanation: Renegotiating the terms of a country's debt with its creditors, often reducing what's owed or extending repayment timelines.

cards.title: Austerity Spending Cuts
cards.realWorldContext: Greece's post-2010 austerity program cut pensions and public spending sharply to satisfy bailout terms, reducing deficits but triggering major unemployment and unrest.
cards.policyExplanation: Reducing government spending (often on pensions, subsidies, or public services) to shrink a budget deficit.

cards.title: Central Bank Currency Peg
cards.realWorldContext: Argentina's 1990s currency board pegged the peso to the US dollar to control inflation. Pegs hold until reserves run low, then often collapse abruptly.
cards.policyExplanation: Fixing a currency's value to another currency (often the US dollar) to control inflation and stabilize expectations.

debrief: Pairing an IMF Bailout with Emergency Capital Controls secures immediate liquidity while stemming capital flight to stabilize domestic currency.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would weigh short-term suffering from austerity against long-term stability, favoring whichever path minimizes total harm.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would object to austerity that cuts pensions and services relied on by the poorest, even if it improves the country's overall finances.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor debt restructuring and market solutions over IMF conditions that constrain a country's sovereign economic choices.

title: Grid Security Cyber Strike
scenario: A state-sponsored cyberattack takes out power grids across two major industrial provinces, threatening national infrastructure and defense readiness.

cards.title: Nationalize Energy Utilities
cards.realWorldContext: Governments have nationalized critical infrastructure during wartime (e.g. rail networks) to guarantee coordinated response, trading market efficiency for direct control.
cards.policyExplanation: The government taking direct ownership and control of energy companies, usually to guarantee coordinated action during a crisis.

cards.title: Private Security Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: Contracting private cybersecurity firms can patch vulnerabilities faster than public agencies, but shifts accountability for critical infrastructure to private actors.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding for private companies to help secure critical infrastructure faster than public agencies alone could.

cards.title: Deploy National Guard
cards.realWorldContext: US state National Guard units include dedicated cyber response teams that have supported real infrastructure attacks, providing trained capacity fast.
cards.policyExplanation: Activating military reserve units for domestic support roles, including responding to infrastructure or security emergencies.

cards.title: Offensive Cyber Retaliation
cards.realWorldContext: 'Hack-back' retaliation is a real and controversial cybersecurity policy debate. Attribution is often uncertain, and retaliation risks escalating a conflict.
cards.policyExplanation: Launching a counter-cyberattack against whoever is believed responsible for the original attack.

cards.title: Emergency Civilian Disaster Relief
cards.realWorldContext: Direct relief funding for affected communities mirrors FEMA's role after infrastructure disasters, prioritizing citizens' immediate needs over rebuilding first.
cards.policyExplanation: Direct financial or material aid sent to affected communities to help them cope with an immediate crisis.

debrief: Deploying the National Guard maintains public order while Nationalizing Utilities mobilizes direct state investment into critical infrastructure repair.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor the fastest restoration of power for the most people, regardless of who controls the fix.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether vulnerable communities without backup power are prioritized in the response.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would be wary of nationalizing utilities, preferring private-sector solutions even during a crisis.

title: Pandemic Zoonotic Outbreak
scenario: A novel respiratory pathogen spreads rapidly through transport hubs. Healthcare facilities in urban districts are near collapse.

cards.title: Mandatory Regional Lockdowns
cards.realWorldContext: Lockdowns were used worldwide during COVID-19 to protect health systems. Effective at slowing transmission, but caused major economic contraction.
cards.policyExplanation: Government orders restricting movement and business activity in specific areas to slow the spread of disease.

cards.title: Universal Vaccine Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: The US 'Operation Warp Speed' funded vaccine development and distribution directly, spreading cost across taxpayers to reach immunity faster.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding that covers the cost of vaccine development and distribution so it's free or cheap for the public.

cards.title: Keep Commercial Ports Open
cards.realWorldContext: Sweden kept commercial activity running longer than most countries during COVID, trading some public health risk for continued trade and lower unemployment.
cards.policyExplanation: Choosing to keep trade and economic activity running during a health crisis, accepting more public health risk in exchange for economic stability.

cards.title: Emergency Hospital Mobilization
cards.realWorldContext: Field hospitals like the one set up in NYC's Javits Center during COVID expanded medical capacity quickly without shutting down the broader economy.
cards.policyExplanation: Rapidly setting up temporary medical facilities to expand treatment capacity without shutting down the broader economy.

cards.title: Patriotic Work Mandates
cards.realWorldContext: Mandating continued labor output echoes historical 'essential worker' policies that prioritized production over individual choice, at real ethical cost.
cards.policyExplanation: Government orders requiring people to keep working in essential roles during a crisis, prioritizing continued production over individual choice.

debrief: Universal Vaccine Subsidies paired with Emergency Hospital Mobilization expands medical bandwidth rapidly without forcing an economic shutdown.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whichever policy saves the most lives, even at real economic cost.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask who bears the burden of lockdowns — often lower-income workers who can't work remotely.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would resist mandates on movement or labor, favoring voluntary measures over state coercion, even during a health crisis.

title: Agrarian Drought Crisis
scenario: A multi-year drought destroys 40% of the grain harvest, sparking severe rural unemployment and skyrocketing food import bills.

cards.title: Strategic Grain Reserve Release
cards.realWorldContext: The US and China both maintain strategic grain reserves, released during shortages to stabilize prices immediately without waiting on new harvests.
cards.policyExplanation: Releasing government-held emergency food stockpiles onto the market to quickly ease shortages.

cards.title: Agricultural Tariff Deregulation
cards.realWorldContext: Lowering food import tariffs, a common shortage response, increases supply from abroad and brings prices down relatively quickly.
cards.policyExplanation: Lowering or removing taxes on imported food, making it cheaper and increasing available supply.

cards.title: Farmer Direct Relief Grants
cards.realWorldContext: Direct payments to farmers, similar to Depression-era US farm relief programs, cushion income loss without directly changing market prices.
cards.policyExplanation: Direct government payments to farmers to offset lost income, without changing market prices.

cards.title: Desalination Infrastructure Loan
cards.realWorldContext: Israel's major investment in desalination after prolonged droughts shows real long-term payoff, though it's slow and capital-intensive.
cards.policyExplanation: Government financing for facilities that convert seawater into fresh water, addressing water scarcity long-term.

cards.title: Mandatory Crop Reallocation
cards.realWorldContext: Centrally planned economies have mandated specific crop production during shortages. It can address scarcity but undermines farmer autonomy and market signals.
cards.policyExplanation: Government orders requiring farmers to grow specific crops the country needs most, overriding their own planting choices.

debrief: Releasing Strategic Grain Reserves directly stabilizes food availability while Tariff Deregulation lowers import costs to protect the nation's bottom line.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whatever gets food to the most people fastest, whether through reserves, imports, or aid.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize struggling farmers and food-insecure households over broad market fixes that help everyone equally.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose mandatory crop reallocation as government overreach into private land and labor decisions.

title: Maritime Trade Blockade
scenario: A dispute over maritime borders halts commercial shipping through a key straits channel, stranding vital industrial exports.

cards.title: Naval Escort Convoys
cards.realWorldContext: Convoy protection for merchant shipping was used in both World Wars and more recently in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea. It restores safe passage but risks military escalation.
cards.policyExplanation: Using military ships to protect merchant vessels traveling through dangerous or blockaded waters.

cards.title: Strategic Bilateral Trade Pivot
cards.realWorldContext: The EU rerouted trade to new energy partners after 2022 to reduce dependence on Russia. It restores solvency but takes time to build new logistics.
cards.policyExplanation: Redirecting trade toward a new partner country to replace a disrupted supply route.

cards.title: International Sanctions Package
cards.realWorldContext: Coordinated sanctions, like those against Russia after 2022, pressure the opposing party diplomatically but often take months to have real effect.
cards.policyExplanation: Coordinated economic penalties imposed on another country to pressure it into changing its behavior.

cards.title: Domestic Industrial Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: Supporting domestic industry to replace blocked imports mirrors wartime industrial mobilization: it protects jobs but is expensive and slow to scale.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding for domestic manufacturers to help them replace goods that can no longer be imported.

cards.title: Seize Foreign Commercial Assets
cards.realWorldContext: Freezing a foreign state's assets, as Western nations did with Russian central bank reserves in 2022, provides leverage but risks major diplomatic fallout.
cards.policyExplanation: Taking control of another country's assets located within your borders, often as leverage in a dispute.

debrief: Deploying Naval Escort Convoys reopens commercial shipping lanes while a Strategic Bilateral Trade Pivot secures financial solvency through alternative trade routes.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor the fastest reopening of trade, regardless of whether it's achieved through force, diplomacy, or new partnerships.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask which citizens are hurt worst by the blockade and prioritize protecting them first.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor market-based solutions like new trade partners over state actions like asset seizures or military escorts.

title: Critical Mineral Export Embargo
scenario: A major foreign supplier freezes exports of refined rare-earth elements, threatening domestic high-tech manufacturing and defense supply chains.

cards.title: Emergency Mining Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: Recent US and EU critical minerals initiatives fund domestic mining to reduce import dependence, though payoff takes years, not months.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding to speed up domestic mining projects and reduce reliance on imported materials.

cards.title: Strategic Stockpile Auction
cards.realWorldContext: The US National Defense Stockpile holds reserves of critical minerals for exactly this scenario: releasing them eases shortages without new production.
cards.policyExplanation: Selling off government-held reserves of a critical material to ease a shortage without waiting for new production.

cards.title: Bilateral Reciprocal Trade Pact
cards.realWorldContext: The US and allies have pursued new mineral supply agreements to diversify away from single-source dependence, a real ongoing trade strategy.
cards.policyExplanation: A trade agreement between two countries that guarantees each side reliable access to specific goods or materials.

cards.title: Domestic Tech Export Tariff
cards.realWorldContext: Restricting exports of finished tech goods to pressure a trading partner mirrors real export-control tools, though it can invite retaliation.
cards.policyExplanation: A tax on exporting finished technology products, used as leverage to pressure a trading partner.

cards.title: Environmental Mining Deregulation
cards.realWorldContext: Loosening environmental permitting to speed up mining approvals accelerates supply, but carries real ecological and community costs debated in actual mining policy.
cards.policyExplanation: Loosening environmental rules around mining to speed up approval and production, at the cost of ecological protections.

debrief: Auctioning strategic mineral reserves bridges immediate manufacturing deficits while negotiating a bilateral trade pact secures long-term raw material imports.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whichever combination restores supply fastest, regardless of long-term dependence.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether the burden of scarcity falls disproportionately on specific industries or communities.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor new trade deals and market diversification over government subsidies or deregulation shortcuts.

title: Housing Market Collapse
scenario: A speculative bubble in urban real estate bursts, wiping out household equity and triggering a wave of mortgage defaults nationwide.

cards.title: Mortgage Relief Program
cards.realWorldContext: The US HAMP program after 2008 modified troubled mortgages to keep families in homes, easing hardship but costing the government billions.
cards.policyExplanation: A government program that modifies mortgage terms so struggling homeowners can afford to keep their homes.

cards.title: Bank Recapitalization Fund
cards.realWorldContext: TARP in 2008 injected public capital directly into failing banks. It stabilized the financial system but was widely seen as bailing out Wall Street over homeowners.
cards.policyExplanation: Public funds injected directly into failing banks to keep them solvent and lending.

cards.title: Foreclosure Moratorium
cards.realWorldContext: Temporary foreclosure freezes, used during COVID-19, prevent mass evictions but leave lenders unable to recover losses in the interim.
cards.policyExplanation: A temporary legal freeze on banks foreclosing on homes, giving struggling owners breathing room.

cards.title: Interest Rate Cut
cards.realWorldContext: Central banks routinely cut rates during housing crashes, as the Fed did after 2008, to make borrowing cheaper and support prices.
cards.policyExplanation: Lowering the cost of borrowing money to make mortgages and loans cheaper across the economy.

cards.title: Let Market Correct Naturally
cards.realWorldContext: Some economists argue intervention only delays necessary corrections; Iceland largely let its banks fail in 2008 rather than bail them out.
cards.policyExplanation: Choosing not to intervene, letting prices and institutions adjust on their own.

debrief: Combining Mortgage Relief Program with Bank Recapitalization Fund is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever combination stabilizes the housing market fastest for the most people, even if it means bailing out banks.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether homeowners at risk of losing their homes are protected before bank shareholders are.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose bailouts, arguing failing institutions and overextended borrowers should face the consequences of market risk.

title: Currency Speculation Attack
scenario: Hedge funds mount a coordinated short-selling attack on the national currency, betting it cannot hold its value against the dollar.

cards.title: Defend the Peg
cards.realWorldContext: The UK spent billions defending the pound against speculators on Black Wednesday in 1992 before abandoning the peg entirely.
cards.policyExplanation: Using national reserves to buy back currency and keep its value fixed against speculators.

cards.title: Float the Currency
cards.realWorldContext: Letting a currency float freely, as the UK ultimately did in 1992, ends a costly defense but causes a sharp, visible devaluation.
cards.policyExplanation: Letting the currency's value move freely based on market supply and demand.

cards.title: Emergency Rate Hike
cards.realWorldContext: Countries facing speculative attacks often hike rates sharply to make holding the currency more attractive, as several Asian economies tried in 1997.
cards.policyExplanation: A sharp, sudden increase in interest rates to make holding the currency more attractive.

cards.title: Impose Capital Controls
cards.realWorldContext: Malaysia imposed capital controls during the 1997 Asian financial crisis rather than follow IMF orthodoxy, drawing criticism but limiting outflows.
cards.policyExplanation: Government limits on how much money can be moved out of the country.

cards.title: Seek IMF Standby Facility
cards.realWorldContext: IMF standby arrangements provide emergency currency support, as used by South Korea in 1997, in exchange for economic reform commitments.
cards.policyExplanation: An emergency line of credit from the IMF, available if a currency crisis worsens.

debrief: Combining Emergency Rate Hike with Seek IMF Standby Facility is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever response stabilizes the economy fastest, regardless of whether it's a peg defense or a float.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask who bears the cost of a currency collapse — often those with the least savings to absorb a shock.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor letting the currency float freely rather than spending reserves to prop up an artificial peg.

title: Tech Stock Bubble Burst
scenario: A speculative rally in technology equities collapses in a single week, erasing trillions in market value and threatening pension funds.

cards.title: Circuit Breaker Trading Halts
cards.realWorldContext: US stock exchanges use circuit breakers that pause trading during steep drops, a tool introduced after the 1987 crash to prevent panic selling.
cards.policyExplanation: Automatic, temporary pauses in stock trading during extreme price drops to prevent panic selling.

cards.title: Pension Fund Backstop
cards.realWorldContext: Governments have occasionally stepped in to guarantee pension obligations when fund assets collapse, protecting retirees at direct fiscal cost.
cards.policyExplanation: A government guarantee to cover pension losses if fund investments collapse.

cards.title: Loosen Margin Requirements
cards.realWorldContext: Reducing how much collateral investors need can ease liquidity crunches, but critics say it enables further speculative risk-taking.
cards.policyExplanation: Reducing how much collateral investors need to trade, freeing up more capital to move.

cards.title: Launch Antitrust Investigation
cards.realWorldContext: Major tech bubbles have often prompted renewed antitrust scrutiny, as seen after the dot-com crash, addressing concentration but adding market uncertainty.
cards.policyExplanation: A government investigation into whether large companies are unfairly dominating a market.

cards.title: Do Nothing, Let Markets Correct
cards.realWorldContext: Some policymakers, echoing Alan Greenspan's early stance on the dot-com bubble, argue markets self-correct and intervention only delays the reckoning.
cards.policyExplanation: Allowing the market to correct on its own without government action.

debrief: Combining Circuit Breaker Trading Halts with Loosen Margin Requirements is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whatever prevents the widest financial damage, even if it means intervening in markets.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether ordinary retirees, not just wealthy investors, are protected from the crash.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would resist government intervention, arguing a market correction should be allowed to run its course.

title: Minimum Wage Standoff
scenario: A push to sharply raise the minimum wage splits the legislature as small businesses warn of mass layoffs and workers demand relief from inflation.

cards.title: Phased Wage Increase
cards.realWorldContext: Many US states have raised minimum wages gradually over several years rather than all at once, softening the shock to small employers.
cards.policyExplanation: Raising the minimum wage gradually over time instead of all at once.

cards.title: Small Business Tax Credits
cards.realWorldContext: Offsetting wage increases with tax credits for small employers is a common compromise used in several state-level minimum wage laws.
cards.policyExplanation: Tax breaks that offset the cost of higher wages for small businesses.

cards.title: Index Wages to Inflation
cards.realWorldContext: Several countries and US states automatically adjust minimum wage to inflation, avoiding repeated political fights but locking in future cost increases.
cards.policyExplanation: Automatically adjusting the minimum wage to keep pace with inflation.

cards.title: Freeze Wages, Cite Business Risk
cards.realWorldContext: Business lobbies have long argued minimum wage freezes protect jobs; opponents note this leaves low-wage workers behind during inflation.
cards.policyExplanation: Keeping wages unchanged to avoid the risk of job losses for businesses.

cards.title: Universal Basic Income Pilot
cards.realWorldContext: Cities like Stockton, California piloted direct cash payments instead of wage mandates, showing promising results but at real fiscal cost.
cards.policyExplanation: Giving people a fixed cash payment regardless of employment status, instead of raising wages.

debrief: Combining Phased Wage Increase with Index Wages to Inflation is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would weigh whether higher wages help more workers than they hurt through potential job losses.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would favor policies that most directly help the lowest-paid workers, even if businesses bear real costs.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose wage mandates entirely, favoring voluntary agreements between employers and workers.

title: Pension Fund Insolvency
scenario: An actuarial review reveals the national public pension system is underfunded by decades, threatening benefits for millions of retirees.

cards.title: Raise Retirement Age
cards.realWorldContext: France's 2023 pension reform raising the retirement age from 62 to 64 sparked massive strikes and protests despite improving fund solvency.
cards.policyExplanation: Requiring people to work and pay into the system longer before they can retire.

cards.title: Increase Payroll Contributions
cards.realWorldContext: Raising payroll tax contributions is a common lever to shore up pension systems, spreading the cost across current workers rather than retirees.
cards.policyExplanation: Increasing how much current workers pay into the pension system.

cards.title: Partial Benefit Cuts
cards.realWorldContext: Greece cut public pensions repeatedly during its debt crisis under bailout terms, restoring solvency but causing significant hardship for retirees.
cards.policyExplanation: Reducing the amount retirees receive from their pensions.

cards.title: General Fund Bailout
cards.realWorldContext: Some US states have used general tax revenue to shore up underfunded pension systems, protecting retirees but straining the broader budget.
cards.policyExplanation: Using general government tax revenue to cover pension shortfalls.

cards.title: Shift to Private Accounts
cards.realWorldContext: Chile's 1980s shift to private pension accounts became a global model, though it later drew criticism for leaving many with inadequate retirement savings.
cards.policyExplanation: Moving retirement savings out of the public system and into individually managed private accounts.

debrief: Combining Increase Payroll Contributions with General Fund Bailout is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whichever reform keeps the pension system solvent for the most people long-term.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would object to benefit cuts that hurt current retirees who can no longer adjust their plans.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor shifting to private accounts, giving individuals more control over their own retirement savings.

title: Trade Deficit Spiral
scenario: A persistent, worsening trade imbalance drains foreign reserves and puts pressure on domestic manufacturers unable to compete with cheap imports.

cards.title: Impose Import Tariffs
cards.realWorldContext: The US imposed steel and aluminum tariffs in 2018 to protect domestic manufacturing, though this raised costs for downstream industries and invited retaliation.
cards.policyExplanation: A tax on imported goods, making them more expensive to encourage buying domestic products.

cards.title: Currency Devaluation
cards.realWorldContext: China has been accused of managing its currency's value to keep exports competitive, a strategy that boosts trade balances but invites accusations of manipulation.
cards.policyExplanation: Deliberately lowering a currency's value to make exports cheaper and more competitive abroad.

cards.title: Domestic Manufacturing Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: The US CHIPS Act subsidized domestic semiconductor manufacturing to reduce import dependence, a costly but targeted industrial policy.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding to help domestic factories compete with cheaper imports.

cards.title: Negotiate New Trade Agreement
cards.realWorldContext: Renegotiating trade terms, as the US did with NAFTA into USMCA, can rebalance trade rules but takes years of negotiation to finalize.
cards.policyExplanation: Renegotiating the terms of trade with another country.

cards.title: Do Nothing, Trust Market Forces
cards.realWorldContext: Mainstream economists have long argued trade deficits self-correct through currency markets over time, though the adjustment can be politically painful.
cards.policyExplanation: Letting currency markets correct the imbalance naturally over time.

debrief: Targeted manufacturing subsidies paired with new trade negotiations address the imbalance without the retaliation risk of broad tariffs.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever fix narrows the trade deficit fastest, even if it raises consumer prices.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether tariffs disproportionately raise costs for lower-income households.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose tariffs and subsidies, preferring free trade with minimal government interference.

title: Cryptocurrency Exchange Collapse
scenario: The nation's largest cryptocurrency exchange collapses overnight amid fraud allegations, wiping out savings for hundreds of thousands of retail investors.

cards.title: Freeze Exchange Assets
cards.realWorldContext: Regulators froze assets tied to FTX after its 2022 collapse to preserve whatever funds remained for eventual creditor recovery.
cards.policyExplanation: Legally locking remaining funds in place so they can't be moved or hidden before an investigation.

cards.title: Criminal Fraud Investigation
cards.realWorldContext: FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried was criminally prosecuted and convicted of fraud, a process that took years but delivered public accountability.
cards.policyExplanation: A formal legal case pursuing criminal charges against those responsible for the collapse.

cards.title: Retail Investor Compensation Fund
cards.realWorldContext: Some jurisdictions have explored compensation funds for retail crypto losses, similar in spirit to securities investor protection funds, though rarely at full value.
cards.policyExplanation: A fund that reimburses at least part of what retail investors lost.

cards.title: Emergency Crypto Regulation
cards.realWorldContext: The EU's MiCA framework, developed after several major collapses, imposes licensing and reserve requirements on crypto exchanges to prevent future failures.
cards.policyExplanation: New rules requiring exchanges to hold reserves and follow licensing requirements.

cards.title: Declare It Buyer Beware
cards.realWorldContext: Some regulators have taken a hands-off stance toward crypto losses, arguing investors knowingly took on unregulated risk — a position that leaves victims without recourse.
cards.policyExplanation: Taking the position that investors knowingly took on risk and are not owed compensation.

debrief: Freezing remaining assets while pursuing a criminal fraud case protects what funds remain and delivers accountability without the state absorbing private losses outright.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whichever response recovers the most funds for the most affected investors.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize compensating smaller retail investors over large institutional ones.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would argue investors accepted the risk of an unregulated market and aren't entitled to a bailout.

title: Manufacturing Automation Layoffs
scenario: A wave of factory automation displaces tens of thousands of manufacturing workers within months, concentrated in a handful of industrial towns.

cards.title: Robot Tax on Automation
cards.realWorldContext: Proposals to tax companies for automating jobs, floated by figures like Bill Gates, aim to fund worker transition programs, though few countries have implemented one.
cards.policyExplanation: A tax on companies that replace workers with automated systems, meant to fund worker transitions.

cards.title: Worker Retraining Program
cards.realWorldContext: Germany's dual vocational training system is often cited as a model for retraining displaced workers into new skilled trades.
cards.policyExplanation: Government-funded training to help displaced workers learn new skills for new jobs.

cards.title: Extended Unemployment Benefits
cards.realWorldContext: Extending jobless benefits during major economic disruptions, as many governments did during COVID, cushions workers but adds fiscal strain.
cards.policyExplanation: Longer-lasting jobless benefits to support workers while they search for new employment.

cards.title: Subsidize Factory Relocation
cards.realWorldContext: Regional development subsidies to relocate industry into affected towns have been used in the US Rust Belt with mixed long-term success.
cards.policyExplanation: Financial incentives to relocate factories and jobs into affected communities.

cards.title: Let the Market Adjust
cards.realWorldContext: Classical economic theory holds that automation-driven displacement is eventually offset by new job creation, though the transition can take a generation.
cards.policyExplanation: Trusting that new jobs will eventually replace the ones lost to automation.

debrief: Combining Robot Tax on Automation with Worker Retraining Program is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would support whichever policy eases the transition for the most displaced workers overall.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize direct support for workers who have the fewest resources to retrain on their own.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would resist a robot tax, arguing automation's economic benefits shouldn't be penalized.

title: Oil Price Shock
scenario: A geopolitical disruption cuts global oil supply overnight, sending fuel prices soaring and threatening transportation and heating costs nationwide.

cards.title: Release Strategic Petroleum Reserve
cards.realWorldContext: The US released oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve in 2022 to ease prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global supply.
cards.policyExplanation: Releasing government-held emergency oil supplies to ease prices immediately.

cards.title: Fuel Subsidy Program
cards.realWorldContext: Many governments subsidize fuel prices during shocks to protect consumers, though this can become a costly, hard-to-remove long-term burden.
cards.policyExplanation: Government payments that lower the price consumers pay for fuel.

cards.title: Emergency Fuel Rationing
cards.realWorldContext: The 1970s oil crisis prompted fuel rationing in several countries, including odd-even license plate purchasing days in the US.
cards.policyExplanation: Formal limits on how much fuel individuals or businesses can purchase.

cards.title: Accelerate Renewable Investment
cards.realWorldContext: Oil shocks have historically accelerated renewable energy investment, as seen after the 1970s crisis spurred early US solar and efficiency programs.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding to speed up the shift toward renewable energy sources.

cards.title: Negotiate Emergency Supply Deal
cards.realWorldContext: Governments often negotiate emergency bilateral energy deals during shortages, similar to Europe's rapid LNG deals after 2022.
cards.policyExplanation: A government-to-government deal securing a reliable, alternative energy supply.

debrief: Combining Release Strategic Petroleum Reserve with Negotiate Emergency Supply Deal is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever response eases fuel costs for the most people fastest.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether relief reaches lower-income households who spend a larger share of income on fuel.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose subsidies and rationing, preferring to let fuel prices adjust naturally.

title: Sovereign Wealth Fund Mismanagement
scenario: An audit reveals the national sovereign wealth fund lost a third of its value through reckless speculative investments, sparking public outrage.

cards.title: Fire Fund Management
cards.realWorldContext: Public outcry over sovereign fund losses has historically forced leadership changes, as seen in several state pension and wealth fund scandals.
cards.policyExplanation: Removing the people responsible for the fund's losses.

cards.title: Independent Oversight Board
cards.realWorldContext: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is governed by strict independent oversight and ethical investment guidelines, widely cited as a model for transparency.
cards.policyExplanation: An independent group that reviews and approves major fund decisions to prevent future mismanagement.

cards.title: Quietly Absorb the Losses
cards.realWorldContext: Some governments have downplayed fund losses to avoid political fallout, a pattern that erodes public trust when the losses eventually surface.
cards.policyExplanation: Choosing not to publicly disclose the losses to avoid political backlash.

cards.title: Public Transparency Reforms
cards.realWorldContext: Requiring public disclosure of fund holdings and performance, as several transparency-focused funds now do, restores accountability at the cost of political exposure.
cards.policyExplanation: Requiring the fund to publicly report its holdings and performance regularly.

cards.title: Liquidate Risky Holdings
cards.realWorldContext: Rapidly selling off speculative assets to limit further losses can lock in a bad price, but stops the bleeding immediately.
cards.policyExplanation: Selling off high-risk investments quickly to stop further losses.

debrief: Combining Fire Fund Management with Independent Oversight Board is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever response restores public trust and fund performance fastest.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would emphasize transparency, since the public — not just fund managers — bears the cost of mismanagement.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would question why a sovereign fund exists at all, preferring capital stay in private hands.

title: Border Migration Surge
scenario: Tens of thousands of migrants arrive at the southern border within weeks, fleeing instability in a neighboring country, overwhelming processing capacity.

cards.title: Expand Processing Centers
cards.realWorldContext: The US has repeatedly expanded temporary processing facilities during migration surges, easing backlogs at significant short-term cost.
cards.policyExplanation: Building out more facilities to process migrants and asylum claims faster.

cards.title: Deploy Border Patrol Surge
cards.realWorldContext: Surging border enforcement personnel during migration spikes is a common US response, improving order but drawing criticism over conditions in detention.
cards.policyExplanation: Sending more enforcement personnel to manage the surge at the border.

cards.title: Regional Resettlement Agreement
cards.realWorldContext: The EU's burden-sharing agreements during the 2015 migration crisis attempted to distribute asylum seekers across member states, with uneven cooperation.
cards.policyExplanation: An agreement with neighboring countries to share responsibility for hosting migrants.

cards.title: Close the Border
cards.realWorldContext: Full border closures, like Title 42 during COVID-19, sharply reduce crossings but face legal challenges and humanitarian criticism.
cards.policyExplanation: Fully closing the border to new arrivals.

cards.title: Address Root Causes Abroad
cards.realWorldContext: US aid programs targeting the economic causes of migration in Central America aim to reduce departures at the source, though results take years to show.
cards.policyExplanation: Funding programs abroad meant to reduce the economic pressures that cause people to migrate.

debrief: Combining Deploy Border Patrol Surge with Regional Resettlement Agreement is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever policy processes the most people fairly and quickly.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize protecting the most vulnerable migrants, regardless of the strain on the system.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor more open movement, seeing strict border closures as an infringement on individual freedom.

title: Cross-Border Water Rights Dispute
scenario: A neighboring country begins diverting a shared river for a new dam project, threatening water supply to millions of downstream farmers and cities.

cards.title: Emergency Water Rationing
cards.realWorldContext: Downstream water shortages from upstream damming have prompted rationing in several river basins, including the Nile and Mekong.
cards.policyExplanation: Government-mandated limits on water use to stretch a shrinking supply.

cards.title: International Arbitration Request
cards.realWorldContext: The International Court of Justice has ruled on transboundary water disputes before, though enforcement of rulings remains difficult.
cards.policyExplanation: Taking the dispute to an international legal body for a binding ruling.

cards.title: Threaten Trade Retaliation
cards.realWorldContext: Egypt has repeatedly signaled economic and diplomatic retaliation over Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam on the Nile, without resorting to force.
cards.policyExplanation: Using trade as leverage to pressure the other country over the water dispute.

cards.title: Fund Desalination Alternative
cards.realWorldContext: Gulf states facing water scarcity have invested heavily in desalination as an alternative to contested freshwater sources.
cards.policyExplanation: Investing in technology that creates fresh water from seawater, reducing reliance on the disputed source.

cards.title: Negotiate Water-Sharing Treaty
cards.realWorldContext: The Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan has managed shared river resources for decades despite broader political tension between the two.
cards.policyExplanation: A formal agreement setting out how the shared water resource will be divided.

debrief: Combining International Arbitration Request with Negotiate Water-Sharing Treaty is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever solution provides water to the most people, even if it means costly infrastructure.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether the poorest downstream communities are protected first.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would prefer negotiated, voluntary agreements over threats of retaliation.

title: Regional Arms Race Escalation
scenario: A rival state announces a major military buildup near a disputed border, prompting calls for a matching response before tensions spiral further.

cards.title: Match Military Spending
cards.realWorldContext: Arms race dynamics, like the Cold War buildup between the US and USSR, often escalate mutually rather than resolving the underlying tension.
cards.policyExplanation: Increasing your own military spending to match a rival's buildup.

cards.title: Propose Bilateral Arms Talks
cards.realWorldContext: Arms control negotiations like SALT and START defused Cold War tensions through verified mutual reductions rather than continued buildup.
cards.policyExplanation: Formal negotiations aimed at both sides reducing weapons together.

cards.title: Strengthen Defensive Alliances
cards.realWorldContext: NATO's collective defense framework under Article 5 is designed to deter aggression by making an attack on one member an attack on all.
cards.policyExplanation: Deepening a mutual-defense agreement with allies to deter aggression.

cards.title: Public Deterrence Statement
cards.realWorldContext: Strong public statements of resolve, without material buildup, are a lower-cost signaling tool used frequently in diplomatic brinkmanship.
cards.policyExplanation: A strong public statement of resolve without an actual military buildup.

cards.title: Preemptive Military Posturing
cards.realWorldContext: Preemptive troop movements near a disputed border risk being read as provocation rather than deterrence, as seen in several historical near-miss crises.
cards.policyExplanation: Moving troops or weapons toward the border preemptively.

debrief: Combining Propose Bilateral Arms Talks with Strengthen Defensive Alliances is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would weigh whether deterrence prevents more harm than an arms buildup risks causing.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether ordinary citizens are made less secure by an arms race neither side really wants.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would be skeptical of large defense spending funded by taxpayers with little say in the matter.

title: Diplomatic Hostage Crisis
scenario: A hostile government detains several of your citizens on disputed espionage charges, demanding a prisoner exchange for their release.

cards.title: Agree to Prisoner Exchange
cards.realWorldContext: Prisoner exchanges, like the 2022 swap that freed Brittney Griner, secure release but are criticized for incentivizing future hostage-taking.
cards.policyExplanation: Trading a prisoner you hold for the release of your detained citizens.

cards.title: Impose Economic Sanctions
cards.realWorldContext: Sanctions are a common response to state-sponsored detention, applying pressure without direct military engagement, though they rarely force quick releases.
cards.policyExplanation: Economic penalties placed on the detaining country to pressure a release.

cards.title: Quiet Backchannel Negotiation
cards.realWorldContext: Many hostage releases are negotiated through discreet diplomatic backchannels rather than public confrontation, preserving both sides' political standing.
cards.policyExplanation: Private, informal negotiations conducted outside of public view.

cards.title: Public Condemnation Campaign
cards.realWorldContext: Public pressure campaigns raise awareness and can mobilize allied support, but risk provoking a detaining government to dig in further.
cards.policyExplanation: Publicly pressuring the detaining government through statements and media attention.

cards.title: Refuse Any Negotiation
cards.realWorldContext: A strict no-negotiation stance, sometimes applied to non-state hostage-takers, avoids setting precedent but leaves detained citizens without a resolution path.
cards.policyExplanation: A firm policy of never negotiating, regardless of the circumstances.

debrief: Pursuing quiet backchannel negotiations while keeping a prisoner exchange on the table resolves the crisis without the precedent-setting risk of public capitulation.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever approach secures release fastest, even if it sets a risky precedent.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize the wellbeing of the detained individuals over abstract policy consistency.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would be wary of sanctions that harm ordinary citizens of the other country for their government's actions.

title: Foreign Election Interference Allegation
scenario: Intelligence agencies report evidence that a foreign government attempted to manipulate the recent national election through disinformation campaigns.

cards.title: Public Intelligence Disclosure
cards.realWorldContext: US intelligence agencies publicly disclosed findings on foreign election interference in 2016 and 2020, informing the public at the cost of politicizing the findings.
cards.policyExplanation: Publicly releasing intelligence findings about the interference.

cards.title: Impose Targeted Sanctions
cards.realWorldContext: The US sanctioned individuals and entities tied to election interference efforts following the 2016 and 2020 elections.
cards.policyExplanation: Financial penalties aimed at those responsible for the interference.

cards.title: Strengthen Election Security Funding
cards.realWorldContext: Congress increased funding for election infrastructure security after 2016, hardening systems against future interference attempts.
cards.policyExplanation: Investing in stronger systems to prevent future election tampering.

cards.title: Diplomatic Protest, No Action
cards.realWorldContext: Formal diplomatic protests without concrete penalties are a lower-risk option, though critics argue they carry little deterrent value.
cards.policyExplanation: A formal diplomatic objection without any real penalty attached.

cards.title: Downplay to Avoid Unrest
cards.realWorldContext: Downplaying interference findings to avoid public panic risks eroding trust further if the full scope later becomes known.
cards.policyExplanation: Choosing not to publicize the findings to avoid causing public alarm.

debrief: Combining Public Intelligence Disclosure with Impose Targeted Sanctions is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever response protects election integrity for the most people.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would argue the public has a right to know, regardless of political discomfort.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would be cautious of government overreach in the name of security, even during a real threat.

title: Territorial Island Dispute
scenario: A neighboring state lands survey teams on a small, resource-rich island your nation also claims, sparking a standoff between coast guard vessels.

cards.title: Deploy Naval Presence
cards.realWorldContext: Naval presence deployments during territorial disputes, common in the South China Sea, assert claims but raise the risk of accidental escalation.
cards.policyExplanation: Sending military ships to visibly assert a territorial claim.

cards.title: File International Tribunal Case
cards.realWorldContext: The Philippines won a 2016 international tribunal ruling against China's South China Sea claims, though China rejected the ruling's enforceability.
cards.policyExplanation: Taking the dispute to an international legal body for a binding ruling.

cards.title: Propose Joint Resource Development
cards.realWorldContext: Joint development zones, used in several maritime disputes, let both claimants share resource revenue without resolving sovereignty outright.
cards.policyExplanation: An agreement to share the disputed resources without resolving who owns the territory.

cards.title: Diplomatic De-escalation Talks
cards.realWorldContext: Bilateral talks to de-escalate maritime standoffs have defused several near-conflicts, buying time without resolving the underlying claim.
cards.policyExplanation: Direct talks aimed at lowering tensions without conceding the claim.

cards.title: Assert Claim by Force
cards.realWorldContext: Forcibly asserting a territorial claim risks military conflict and international condemnation, a step most disputing states have historically avoided.
cards.policyExplanation: Using military force to physically take control of the disputed territory.

debrief: Proposing joint resource development while opening de-escalation talks manages the standoff without conceding the claim or risking direct confrontation.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever approach avoids conflict while securing the most benefit from the disputed resources.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether the dispute's resolution accounts for affected local communities, not just national pride.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor peaceful resolution over state assertion of force in property disputes.

title: Peacekeeping Mission Overextension
scenario: Your nation's peacekeeping troops abroad face a sudden escalation in local violence, and casualties are mounting faster than reinforcements can arrive.

cards.title: Send Reinforcements
cards.realWorldContext: Reinforcing overwhelmed peacekeeping missions, as the UN did in several Balkans deployments, stabilizes the mission but escalates cost and risk.
cards.policyExplanation: Sending more troops to support an overwhelmed peacekeeping mission.

cards.title: Withdraw Troops Immediately
cards.realWorldContext: The rapid 1994 withdrawal of peacekeepers from Rwanda amid escalating violence is widely cited as a failure that allowed the genocide to proceed.
cards.policyExplanation: Pulling troops out of the mission entirely.

cards.title: Request UN Mandate Expansion
cards.realWorldContext: Expanding a peacekeeping mission's mandate to allow more assertive intervention, as eventually happened in Bosnia, requires lengthy Security Council approval.
cards.policyExplanation: Asking for approval to expand what peacekeepers are allowed to do.

cards.title: Shift to Air Support Only
cards.realWorldContext: Providing air support without ground reinforcement reduces risk to personnel but limits the mission's ability to protect civilians on the ground.
cards.policyExplanation: Supporting the mission from the air instead of adding ground troops.

cards.title: Negotiate Local Ceasefire
cards.realWorldContext: Direct negotiation with local factions for a temporary ceasefire has bought time for peacekeeping forces to stabilize in several past conflicts.
cards.policyExplanation: Direct talks with local factions to pause the fighting temporarily.

debrief: Combining Request UN Mandate Expansion with Negotiate Local Ceasefire is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever choice saves the most lives, including both peacekeepers and civilians.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would argue the most vulnerable civilians deserve protection even if it's costly to provide.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would question the cost and legitimacy of extended foreign military commitments funded by taxpayers.

title: Trade War Retaliation
scenario: A major trading partner imposes steep tariffs on your exports after a prolonged dispute, threatening thousands of manufacturing jobs at home.

cards.title: Retaliatory Tariffs
cards.realWorldContext: The US-China trade war saw both sides impose escalating retaliatory tariffs from 2018 onward, raising costs for consumers on both sides.
cards.policyExplanation: Imposing your own tariffs in response to another country's tariffs.

cards.title: Seek WTO Dispute Resolution
cards.realWorldContext: The World Trade Organization's dispute settlement process offers a formal path to challenge tariffs, though rulings can take years to resolve.
cards.policyExplanation: Filing a formal complaint with the World Trade Organization to challenge the tariffs legally.

cards.title: Subsidize Affected Exporters
cards.realWorldContext: The US provided direct payments to farmers hurt by retaliatory tariffs during the 2018-2019 trade war to offset lost export revenue.
cards.policyExplanation: Direct payments to exporters who are losing money because of the tariffs.

cards.title: Diversify Export Markets
cards.realWorldContext: Countries facing trade disputes often accelerate deals with alternative partners, as several nations did to reduce reliance on any single market.
cards.policyExplanation: Finding new countries to trade with to reduce reliance on the original partner.

cards.title: Back Down, Accept Terms
cards.realWorldContext: Accepting unfavorable trade terms to end a dispute quickly avoids further economic damage but can invite future pressure from the same partner.
cards.policyExplanation: Accepting the other country's trade terms to end the dispute quickly.

debrief: Combining Retaliatory Tariffs with Seek WTO Dispute Resolution is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever approach ends the trade war fastest with the least total economic harm.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether retaliatory tariffs disproportionately hurt lower-income consumers.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose tariffs altogether, favoring free trade regardless of what the other country does.

title: Alliance Treaty Obligation Crisis
scenario: A treaty ally is attacked by a hostile neighbor and formally invokes a mutual defense clause, requesting immediate military support.

cards.title: Fulfill Treaty Obligation
cards.realWorldContext: NATO's Article 5 has been invoked once, after 9/11, committing member states to collective defense obligations at real material and political cost.
cards.policyExplanation: Sending your own troops to defend an ally under attack, as a treaty requires.

cards.title: Provide Arms, Not Troops
cards.realWorldContext: Western support for Ukraine after 2022 largely took the form of arms and financial aid rather than direct troop deployment, avoiding direct confrontation.
cards.policyExplanation: Supporting an ally with weapons and funding, but not troops.

cards.title: Seek UN Security Council Backing
cards.realWorldContext: Seeking Security Council authorization for military action adds international legitimacy, though a veto from a permanent member can block it entirely.
cards.policyExplanation: Seeking formal approval from the UN before taking action.

cards.title: Delay, Cite Domestic Politics
cards.realWorldContext: Delaying treaty commitments due to domestic political resistance risks damaging alliance credibility for future crises.
cards.policyExplanation: Slowing down your response due to political resistance at home.

cards.title: Offer Humanitarian Aid Only
cards.realWorldContext: Providing humanitarian rather than military aid is a common lower-commitment response when full treaty obligations carry high domestic political risk.
cards.policyExplanation: Providing only humanitarian, non-military assistance.

debrief: Combining Provide Arms, Not Troops with Seek UN Security Council Backing is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would weigh the cost of fulfilling the treaty against the harm of appearing unreliable to allies.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would ask whether the citizens of the attacked ally are being protected fairly.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would be skeptical of costly foreign military commitments, even under treaty obligation.

title: Refugee Resettlement Standoff
scenario: Neighboring countries close their borders to a growing refugee population fleeing conflict, leaving your nation as one of the few remaining entry points.

cards.title: Open Emergency Resettlement Camps
cards.realWorldContext: Jordan and Turkey have hosted massive refugee camps during the Syrian civil war, absorbing large populations at significant strain to public services.
cards.policyExplanation: Setting up emergency camps to house large numbers of refugees.

cards.title: Request International Burden-Sharing
cards.realWorldContext: UNHCR-coordinated resettlement programs distribute refugee responsibility across countries, though participation has historically been inconsistent.
cards.policyExplanation: Asking other countries to help share the responsibility of hosting refugees.

cards.title: Cap Admissions at Set Quota
cards.realWorldContext: Many countries set annual refugee admission caps to manage capacity, a policy that provides predictability but leaves others without protection.
cards.policyExplanation: Setting a hard limit on how many refugees will be accepted.

cards.title: Fund Regional Host Countries
cards.realWorldContext: The EU has funded neighboring countries like Turkey to host refugees rather than accepting larger numbers directly, a widely debated tradeoff.
cards.policyExplanation: Paying nearby countries to host refugees instead of accepting them directly.

cards.title: Close the Border Entirely
cards.realWorldContext: Full border closures during refugee crises, as seen in parts of the 2015 European migration crisis, reduce strain domestically but leave people without safe passage.
cards.policyExplanation: Fully closing the border to refugees.

debrief: Combining Request International Burden-Sharing with Cap Admissions at Set Quota is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever approach helps the most refugees at the lowest overall cost.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize protecting the most vulnerable refugees, even if it strains domestic resources.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor voluntary private and community sponsorship over government-run resettlement programs.

title: Judicial Independence Crisis
scenario: The executive branch proposes legislation to gain greater control over judicial appointments, prompting mass protests and warnings from legal scholars.

cards.title: Withdraw the Legislation
cards.realWorldContext: Israel's government partially paused judicial overhaul legislation in 2023 after mass protests, easing tension without fully abandoning reform goals.
cards.policyExplanation: Pulling back a proposal that would have reduced judicial independence.

cards.title: Push Legislation Through
cards.realWorldContext: Poland's judicial reforms in the late 2010s, pushed through despite EU objections, drew years of legal and diplomatic conflict over rule-of-law concerns.
cards.policyExplanation: Passing the law despite public opposition.

cards.title: Propose Independent Review Commission
cards.realWorldContext: Independent commissions to review judicial reform proposals have been used to slow contentious changes and build broader consensus.
cards.policyExplanation: Forming an independent group to review the proposal before it moves forward.

cards.title: National Referendum on Reform
cards.realWorldContext: Putting contested constitutional changes to a public referendum, as some countries have done, transfers the decision directly to voters.
cards.policyExplanation: Putting the decision directly to a public vote.

cards.title: Crack Down on Protests
cards.realWorldContext: Suppressing protests against judicial reform, as seen in several democratic backsliding cases, tends to deepen the very legitimacy crisis it's meant to end.
cards.policyExplanation: Using force to suppress protests against the proposal.

debrief: Proposing an independent review commission slows the process enough to rebuild consensus without fully abandoning reform or escalating into a legitimacy crisis.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would weigh whether the reform's benefits to governance outweigh the unrest it causes.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would be deeply skeptical of any measure that concentrates power and undermines checks on government.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would strongly oppose reducing judicial independence, seeing it as a core check on state power.

title: Press Freedom Crackdown Backlash
scenario: New restrictions on investigative journalism spark international condemnation and a wave of resignations at major state-adjacent media outlets.

cards.title: Repeal the Restrictions
cards.realWorldContext: Governments facing sustained press freedom backlash have occasionally repealed restrictive laws to restore international standing and domestic legitimacy.
cards.policyExplanation: Removing the restrictions on journalism that caused the backlash.

cards.title: Maintain Restrictions, Cite Security
cards.realWorldContext: National security justifications for press restrictions are common globally, from wartime censorship to modern-day 'fake news' laws, and are frequently contested.
cards.policyExplanation: Keeping the restrictions in place, justified by national security concerns.

cards.title: Create Press Ombudsman Office
cards.realWorldContext: Independent press ombudsman offices, used in several democracies, mediate disputes between government and media without direct censorship power.
cards.policyExplanation: An independent office that mediates disputes between government and media.

cards.title: Offer State Media Subsidies
cards.realWorldContext: Subsidizing state-aligned outlets while restricting independent press has been used to shape the media landscape in several countries, drawing criticism over bias.
cards.policyExplanation: Government funding for media outlets that support official positions.

cards.title: International Press Freedom Pledge
cards.realWorldContext: Signing onto international press freedom commitments, as tracked by groups like Reporters Without Borders, signals intent though enforcement mechanisms are limited.
cards.policyExplanation: Formally committing to international press freedom standards.

debrief: Combining Repeal the Restrictions with Create Press Ombudsman Office is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would weigh whether restrictions genuinely improve security enough to justify limiting free expression.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would be wary of restrictions that disproportionately silence marginalized voices.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would strongly oppose any restriction on press freedom as a core violation of individual rights.

title: Public Sector Strike Wave
scenario: Teachers, nurses, and transit workers launch a coordinated general strike over stagnant wages, paralyzing major cities for a second week.

cards.title: Negotiate Wage Increase
cards.realWorldContext: Negotiated wage settlements have ended most major public sector strikes historically, including the UK's 2023 nurses' and rail strikes.
cards.policyExplanation: Agreeing to raise wages to end the strike.

cards.title: Declare Strike Illegal, Order Return
cards.realWorldContext: President Reagan fired striking air traffic controllers in the 1981 PATCO strike after declaring it illegal, a move that reshaped US labor relations for decades.
cards.policyExplanation: Using legal authority to declare the strike illegal and order workers back.

cards.title: Bring In Temporary Replacement Workers
cards.realWorldContext: Using replacement workers during strikes maintains services but is broadly seen as escalatory and has fueled longer, more bitter labor disputes historically.
cards.policyExplanation: Hiring temporary workers to keep services running during the strike.

cards.title: Independent Wage Arbitration
cards.realWorldContext: Binding arbitration panels have resolved major public sector disputes, such as several transit strikes, by having a neutral party set final terms.
cards.policyExplanation: Sending the wage dispute to a neutral third party to decide the outcome.

cards.title: Wait Out the Strike
cards.realWorldContext: Some governments have chosen to wait out strikes rather than negotiate, betting public pressure will force workers back, a strategy that risks prolonging disruption.
cards.policyExplanation: Refusing to negotiate and waiting for the strike to end on its own.

debrief: Combining Negotiate Wage Increase with Independent Wage Arbitration is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever resolution restores public services fastest with the least total disruption.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would side with workers seeking fair wages over measures that suppress their right to strike.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would support workers' right to strike, but be wary of government forcing any particular wage outcome.

title: Urban Housing Shortage Protests
scenario: Skyrocketing rents in the capital spark tent encampments and mass protests demanding immediate government action on housing affordability.

cards.title: Impose Rent Control
cards.realWorldContext: New York City's long-standing rent control system protects existing tenants but is widely debated for discouraging new housing construction.
cards.policyExplanation: Legally capping how much landlords can raise rent.

cards.title: Fast-Track Zoning Reform
cards.realWorldContext: Cities like Minneapolis have loosened single-family zoning to allow denser housing, a slower fix that increases supply over time.
cards.policyExplanation: Changing zoning laws to allow more housing to be built.

cards.title: Public Housing Construction
cards.realWorldContext: Vienna's large public housing program is often cited as a model for keeping a majority of residents in affordable, government-built units.
cards.policyExplanation: The government directly building affordable housing.

cards.title: Clear Encampments
cards.realWorldContext: Encampment clearances during housing crises, common in several major US cities, address visible disorder but don't resolve the underlying shortage.
cards.policyExplanation: Removing homeless encampments from public spaces.

cards.title: Housing Voucher Expansion
cards.realWorldContext: The US Section 8 housing voucher program subsidizes private rent for low-income tenants, a widely used but chronically underfunded approach.
cards.policyExplanation: Government subsidies that help low-income renters afford private housing.

debrief: Combining Impose Rent Control with Fast-Track Zoning Reform is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever policy houses the most people effectively, regardless of market impact.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize the housing security of the poorest residents over overall market efficiency.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would oppose rent control, favoring zoning reform that lets the market build more supply.

title: Education Funding Referendum Failure
scenario: Voters reject a ballot measure that would have raised property taxes to fund public schools, leaving the district facing deep budget cuts.

cards.title: Cut Non-Essential Programs
cards.realWorldContext: School districts facing budget shortfalls commonly cut arts, sports, and elective programs first, a pattern seen across many US districts.
cards.policyExplanation: Reducing spending on non-core programs like arts and sports.

cards.title: Statewide Emergency Funding
cards.realWorldContext: State governments sometimes step in with emergency education funding when local referendums fail, shifting the fiscal burden upward.
cards.policyExplanation: The state government stepping in to cover the funding gap.

cards.title: Consolidate School Districts
cards.realWorldContext: Merging smaller districts to cut administrative costs is a common response to funding shortfalls, though it often faces fierce local opposition.
cards.policyExplanation: Merging smaller school districts to reduce administrative costs.

cards.title: Corporate Education Partnership
cards.realWorldContext: Some districts have turned to corporate sponsorships and partnerships to fill funding gaps, raising concerns about commercial influence in classrooms.
cards.policyExplanation: Accepting corporate sponsorship to fill funding gaps.

cards.title: Re-run the Referendum
cards.realWorldContext: Districts sometimes bring a revised funding measure back to voters after a failed referendum, betting a smaller ask will pass.
cards.policyExplanation: Asking voters to approve a new, revised funding measure.

debrief: Combining Corporate Education Partnership with Re-run the Referendum is the path that actually clears every threshold here — the other pairings look reasonable individually but leave at least one goal short.

philosopherReactions.utilitarian: Would favor whichever funding fix serves the most students effectively.
philosopherReactions.rawlsian: Would prioritize protecting students in the lowest-funded schools first.
philosopherReactions.libertarian: Would favor local control and voluntary funding over state intervention or corporate partnerships.

title: Police Reform Standoff
scenario: After a high-profile incident of police misconduct, activists demand sweeping reforms while police unions warn of a recruitment and morale crisis.

cards.title: Independent Oversight Board
cards.realWorldContext: Civilian oversight boards for police conduct have been established in many major US cities following high-profile misconduct cases.
cards.policyExplanation: An independent civilian group that reviews police conduct.

cards.title: Increase Body Camera Funding
cards.realWorldContext: Body camera programs expanded rapidly after the 2014 Ferguson protests, improving accountability though implementation and footage access vary widely.
cards.policyExplanation: Expanding the use of body cameras to increase accountability.

cards.title: Reallocate Funds to Social Services
cards.realWorldContext: Some cities shifted portions of police budgets toward mental health and social services after 2020, a contested reform with mixed early results.
cards.policyExplanation: Shifting some police funding toward mental health and social services.

cards.title: Increase Police Funding and Staffing
cards.realWorldContext: Other cities responded to rising crime concerns by increasing police budgets and hiring, prioritizing capacity over reform-focused changes.
cards.policyExplanation: Increasing police budgets and hiring more officers.

cards.title: Defend Current Practices Publicly
